about: Every algorithm the site runs, once. tools/site/build_pages.py lists them by field on Science (#algorithms) and, in each homepage band's information panel, those with that band in 'bands' (world: the band's drawn world; piece: its live figure; arrival: the transition into it, scrolled or clicked).

algorithms.name: Depth-first maze carving
algorithms.what: A random spanning tree of the screen’s cells: the carver steps to an unvisited neighbour until it is boxed in, then backs up, which makes long winding corridors.
algorithms.where: Clicking into About Me, Résumé or Contact

algorithms.name: Stateless instanced particles
algorithms.what: Thousands of cubes, streamlines, film strips, drops, shards and ink strokes, one draw call per kind; each position is a pure function of the scroll, so scrolling back un-builds the scene exactly.

algorithms.name: Greedy list scheduling
algorithms.what: Where and when each of the vortex’s cubes lands: landing slots come in the order the cubes leave, and each goes, through a priority queue, to the cell first in the building order (low and outward first) of those whose paper has already gone. So the bottom corners are built first, then upward and inward, and no cube lands on paper. It is planned once per screen size and handed to the shaders as a small texture.

algorithms.name: Paint finding its own land: competing fronts
algorithms.what: The blotches look random, but each is the colour of the land where it fell (the hardwoods’ yellows, oranges and reds; the spruce and fir’s green; white high up), and soon its paint creeps out over a 256 × 256 grid of the map by a multi-source Dijkstra: each cell taken by whichever front reaches it first, a front moving fast through land of its own kind and 2.6 times slower across any other, never into water; its speed found by the secant method so that the canvas is painted by a fixed moment. Meanwhile each blotch draws back off land not its own, its edge sliding along the contour lines, and melts into the paint around it; a glossy bead rides each front, and behind it the colour it brought gives way to the land’s own, laid on in strokes along the contours. The lakes are struck in last, in blue, each from its deepest point. Then the painting rises into relief and becomes the land.

algorithms.name: Precomputed fields
algorithms.what: The ice’s geometry and padded arrival atlases are prepared in a worker. The vortex schedule, ink reach and click maze are also prepared once and read from textures.

algorithms.name: Dynamic resolution
algorithms.what: A feedback loop on frame time: the renderer steps its detail, then its resolution, down when frames run long (a run of slow frames, or too large a share of them missing their frame over the last second) and back up when they are quick, and hands the pages back to their CSS art if even half resolution is too slow.

algorithms.name: Latest-intent navigation
algorithms.what: Every click or history step is an intent with its own abortable fetch; a newer one cancels the older, so the page you land on is always the last one asked for.

algorithms.name: Painter’s algorithm
algorithms.what: The 48 peaks are drawn tallest first, so nearer, lower ones overlap them as in a real range.
algorithms.where: The 48 skyline, on the homepage and Outdoors

algorithms.name: Legal-move generation and SAN parsing
algorithms.what: Games are read move by move from standard algebraic notation into positions, each move checked against the rules (chess.js).
algorithms.where: The Scotch on the homepage, the replay boards on Chess

algorithms.name: Live data with a saved fallback
algorithms.what: Ratings and games are read live from Chess.com; if that fails, the last good answer saved in this browser is shown, with its date.

algorithms.name: The Burgers vortex
algorithms.what: An exact solution of the Navier–Stokes equations: fluid drawn in toward an axis spins faster as it closes in, keeping its angular momentum, and is stretched along the axis. Scrolled, the vortex stands on the foot of the screen and grows taller; the page is gathered into cubes up the screen behind its top, each height over a long window, so some cubes lag behind. Each cube goes round the vortex one and a half to four and a half times, rising with the wind, and is thrown down and out onto the page it builds. Clicked, the cubes come out of the axis at the link and spiral away to build the page. Every cell sends one cube and receives one.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Science, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Density waves
algorithms.what: The ring’s cubes bunch into five swarms, as stars bunch into a galaxy’s spiral arms: each cube’s angle is drawn toward the nearest crest of a wave that turns with the wind, so the swarms keep turning, even while the page is still, as cubes pass through them.

algorithms.name: Divergence-free vortex field
algorithms.what: Three layers of drifting vortex cells, the curl of a stream function, so whatever follows it swirls without bunching up.

algorithms.name: Gravity’s spots: the Jeans instability
algorithms.what: Once a remnant’s gas has cooled it is unstable to its own gravity. A region larger than the Jeans length, λ_J = c √(π / Gρ), collapses; a smaller one is held up by its pressure and its turbulence (c² = c_s² + σ²/3). So the gas breaks into clumps about λ_J apart, closer where it is dense: many along the bright filaments, a few in the thin gas between, larger where the gas is hotter or more turbulent (a Poisson disc of varying radius, densest first). Each clump gathers the gas of its own cell (the points nearer it than any other, in Jeans lengths) and falls in on itself in free fall, t_ff = √(3π / 32Gρ), so the dense collapse first; a uniform sphere falls in all at once (r = r₀ cos²β, with t/t_ff = (β + sin β cos β)/(π/2)), so the gas of each cell is seen gathering toward its middle, its light squeezed brighter while the lanes between cells go dark, until it snaps into a drop of its volume with a soft bloom. First the pattern shows faintly, its contrast growing as e^{σt}. Its drop’s mass is its cell’s light times its depth, about λ_J too: the Jeans mass, ρλ_J³. The plan mirrors the shader’s gas exactly (the same hashed three-dimensional noise), so the clumps form on the filaments that are drawn. Artistic: water from a remnant’s gas.

algorithms.name: Every drop a lens
algorithms.what: A drop looks off its axis toward the far side, so what it shows (the remnant behind it) is inverted and minified, its colour deepest at its middle (the deepest water), with a crescent of gathered light, a glint and the bright thread of its contact line; a clump’s drop also glows with the gas it gathered, and one sitting on Science’s chrome shows the mirror under it. Artistic: a star’s bead holding its star’s light.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Racing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Supernovae and planetary nebulae
algorithms.what: Science’s sky has a dozen supergiants, each coloured as a black body: Planck’s law integrated against the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions, red at 3,400 K, blue-white at 30,000 K. Moving on to Racing, seven of them end (four on a phone), the set spread farthest apart, so each remnant has room of its own and only the outer fringes of neighbours cross, in an order that is not a sweep across or down the screen. Red supergiants are the progenitors of type II-P supernovae, so the red explode as well as the blue. Each pulses faster and faster, dims as its core collapses, then breaks out in a flash that swells rather than pops, fading along the light curve of nickel-56 decaying to cobalt-56 (mean lives 8.8 and 111.3 days, compressed but in proportion), the rest of the scene dimming a little as an eye adapts; a light echo races out through the dust, and the gas near it flares in [O III], then glows in Hα as it recombines. Each remnant is a sphere seen through: it expands freely (R ∝ t), then as a Sedov–Taylor blast wave (R ∝ t^⅖), sweeping the gas round it into its shell and leaving a dark cavity. The shell is drawn by integrating along the line of sight, so it is brightest at its limb (√(1 − ρ²) − √(a² − ρ²) through each half), its gas in wisps of three-dimensional turbulence in its front half and its back half both, its inner edge rippled into Rayleigh–Taylor fingers where the ejecta push into it, knots of ejecta within lit by the reverse shock, the forward shock a thin bright rim; where two shells meet, a brighter arc. Its structure expands with it (homologous) and it cools as it grows. They differ by their physics, not their shapes: a hot progenitor’s remnant glows more in [O III], a cool one’s in Hα and [S II]. Their lines are shown as narrowband images show them, in the Hubble palette: Hα and [S II] gold and amber, [O III] teal. Artistic: the pace, compressed from millennia to a scroll.
algorithms.where: Science’s sky, and arriving at Racing by scroll

algorithms.name: Cold from the card: freezing drops
algorithms.what: Racing’s card appears in its own place as a ghost of cold glass, and a freezing front spreads out from it, its isochrones the card’s own rounded rectangle grown outward, wavy. A drop it reaches is supercooled: ice shoots through it at once (recalescence), so it flashes milky; then it freezes through from its contact line inward, clear and glassy behind the front, in a time that grows as the square of its radius (the Stefan problem: the latent heat has to leave through the ice already frozen). Water expands as it freezes, so the last of it is pushed up into a point at the apex, a glint (the tip singularity of freezing drops, Marín et al. 2014). Then it splits along ice’s prism planes, 60° apart, ice Ih being hexagonal, into a few sectors, a large drop also across them, concentrically; a star’s bead freezes whole; Science’s chrome drops break finer, into mirror pieces, each still curved as the sphere it was. Artistic: the speed of the front.

algorithms.name: The vacuum: shards along the field lines
algorithms.what: Racing’s card draws everything in. The screen’s frame is charged one way and the card the other, a little more strongly, so every field line ends on the card (a two-dimensional Coulomb field, softened, tabulated and read bilinearly); each shard’s line is traced with fourth-order Runge–Kutta from where it split. Each moves overdamped, its speed in proportion to the field, so it starts slowly and quickens as it nears the card; its line is kept at equal steps of its time, so the steps between are its speed. It turns to lie along the field (the torque on its induced dipole), spins about it so its face flashes as it sweeps the light, stretches with its speed and is lifted toward the camera mid-flight; its cleavage faces split the light into its colours; it flares as it fuses. The line it rides is lit just behind it, and one line in four glows faintly as the field builds, a magnet’s filings. The old world drains in along the same lines, drawn by line integral convolution (what is at a point now came from upstream along its line, smeared along it), and a place is empty once what was there has reached the card: Racing’s world shows behind, at night. Near the card first, so freezing, splitting and the pull go out from it as one wave.

algorithms.name: Every star accounted for
algorithms.what: Science’s small stars are placed by a hash, three layers of them, and the plan of the transition into Racing repeats that hash in float32 so it knows every one. A GPU’s rounding is not quite float32’s, so each hash is read through a triangle wave, 1 − |2h − 1|, uniform still but continuous where it wraps: the plan’s stars and the screen’s then agree to a third of a pixel. As the remnants cool each star condenses at its own random time into a bead of clear water full of its light, the bigger stars into bigger beads (one that falls on a clump’s drop joins it); the front from Racing’s card freezes each whole, and it leaves as a single point of light, a shooting star down its field line into the card. Artistic: what the stars become.

algorithms.name: A click: the story about the click
algorithms.what: Clicked, the same story plays about the click in two and a half seconds. A star dies at the click: its core beats, collapses and breaks out, and its light races out as a ring, lighting the remnants’ gas over Science’s sky as it passes, which covers the old page. Gravity’s spots gather the gas into drops, nearest the click first, as the stars condense into beads; the cold spreads out from the click, each drop freezing and splitting; the click draws everything in. A point sink’s field in two dimensions falls as 1/r, so a shard moving overdamped has r² falling steadily, r = r₀√(1 − t/T), its flight T growing as the square of how far out it was, and every shard is home before the page changes. Where everything has gone Racing shows, at night, and the light gathers at the click, a new star; once the new page is in, it goes out as a ring of dawn, and the page opens behind it (the window the page shows through follows the ring). Artistic: the speeds.

algorithms.name: The card takes the light in, and gives it back
algorithms.what: As its shards fuse into Racing’s card their light spreads through its glass from where each lands, every point lit by the first to reach it (a clock over the card: the earliest arrival plus the distance over the spread), in the arriving colours, the dark glass filling. When it has taken everything in it gives its light back: a ring of light goes out from it across Racing, as the supernovae’s did at the start, dawn behind its thin bright front, then Racing’s day; the card cools to glacier white and anneals into Racing’s glass card. Artistic: the light’s round trip, and the page’s text condensing from frost.

algorithms.name: Narrowband false colour
algorithms.what: Telescopes photograph a nebula one emission line at a time and give each line a colour; the Hubble palette sends sulphur, hydrogen and oxygen to red, green and blue, and balanced, its nebulae come out gold and teal. Science takes that mapping for everything: its page and experiments, its sky and liquid chrome, and the nebulae of the transition into Racing, whose drops and shards inherit their colours, down to the light Racing’s card takes in. One source (palette.js) feeds the stylesheet, the shaders and the experiments; the nebulae, lit in linear light, take its colours converted from display values.
algorithms.where: Science, its homepage band, and arriving at Racing

algorithms.name: Thin-film interference
algorithms.what: Light reflected from the top and bottom of a thin layer interferes, so the colour depends on its thickness and the angle you look from.
algorithms.where: The wing scales on Science (summed with CIE colour matching); the liquid chrome’s sheen, a stylised oxide film in Science’s gold and teal; the iridized glass in Outdoors’ window, turning with the angle to the lantern

algorithms.name: Fresnel reflection and Blinn–Phong highlights
algorithms.what: Surfaces reflect more at grazing angles; highlights come from the half-vector between the light and the eye.
algorithms.where: The chrome, the ice, the gilt, the lakes

algorithms.name: Caustics
algorithms.what: Light focused by moving water or rippled ice: an iterated trigonometric warp under the glacier.

algorithms.name: A drop of paint on a canvas
algorithms.what: Racing’s white ice settles into a primed canvas, and thick paint lands on it a drop at a time, slowly at first and then quicker. Each drop spreads to about 0.9 We^¼ times its own radius (Clanet’s scaling, We the Weber number: how hard its inertia pushes against its surface tension), fast and then slowing as √t, overshooting a little and drawing back; its rim, decelerating, breaks into N ≈ √We / (4√3) fingers (Allen: the Rayleigh–Taylor instability of the rim), whose tips pinch off satellite drops (Rayleigh–Plateau), with a fine spray thrown farther; a drop that comes in at a slant stretches its splash and throws its spray downrange. Before it lands, its shadow closes in on it. The paint is impasto: its thickness, built up at the rim, lit as relief from the upper left (its slope from the screen’s derivatives), with a wet gloss that dries and the shadow its rim casts. Artistic: the drops’ count, sizes and colours, the canvas’s weave.

algorithms.name: The White Mountains and their water
algorithms.what: A heightfield of the 48 four-thousand footers at their true latitudes, longitudes and heights: each a massif with concave flanks, neighbours in a range joined by ridges sagging to their cols, a highland of lesser mountains between (ridged noise), then carved by running water, hydraulic erosion by tens of thousands of droplets that pick up sediment where they run fast and steep and drop it where they slow (Beyer’s model), so ravines cut the slopes; each summit is set back to its surveyed height. Water lies level: twenty ponds and tarns are cut where they really are (Lakes of the Clouds, Lonesome Lake, Echo Lake and the rest), each on the flattest bench near its place, a bowl with a lip below and a headwall above as a glacier leaves them, and the lowland’s bigger hollows hold ponds at their bottoms; each is filled to a flat surface by a priority flood (Barnes, Lehman and Mulla), so its shore follows the contour. Built once, off the main thread. Artistic: the shapes between the summits, the water drawn larger than life, the vertical exaggeration (twice).

algorithms.name: A flight over a heightfield
algorithms.what: Every pixel casts a ray from a camera that hangs over the painting while it is made, then dives to fly past Franconia Ridge, along the Garfield Ridge and over the Pemigewasset Wilderness, and turns to the Presidential Range: the ray steps through the heightfield until it meets the ground and refines the hit by bisection; a second march toward the sun gives soft shadows. The studio’s light becomes the sun as the painting rises, coming round to a low October afternoon; the light is sun, sky and bounce, the air an exponential haze integrated along each ray, thicker low down, with mist in the valleys and cloud shadows drifting. The forest is single crowns, Voronoi cells a dozen metres across (spruce and fir dark and pointed, the hardwoods rounded and each its own colour, the shadow each casts on the forest floor) in stands and groves, hemlock along the streams; above the treeline krummholz, sedge and lichen, granite with dark streaks down its slabs, October’s first snow on the highest summits. Lakes lie level, their colour by depth, rippled where the wind gusts, and mirror the mountains: a second, shorter march back up the reflected ray. The fine relief is mipmapped by each sample’s footprint, so far ground does not shimmer.

algorithms.name: Contour lines, leaded
algorithms.what: Looking straight down, the map draws its own contour lines, every 200 ft and stronger every 1,000 ft, at the terrain’s true heights, low to high as if a lake were rising; the 48 summits are marked and the Pemi Loop’s trail dashed in. Then the land settles flat into its map and dusk falls on it, and the contours at the window’s band heights straighten onto its square module (each line the zero of a blend of the contour’s signed distance and the leading’s) and thicken into came; the last light passes through the glass band by band, low to high, sweeping in from the west, each pane flaring as it takes it, and the summits glow red in the order they were climbed.

algorithms.name: Molten lead along the came
algorithms.what: Clicked, Outdoors’ window is leaded from the click: a bead of molten lead touches down and runs out along the window’s real came, round its corners and through its joints, white-hot at its tip and cooling behind to bronze, while the old page dims under it into the window’s dark glass. When it reaches each joint is a Dijkstra over the leading on screen (the module’s cells, each band edge joining the midpoints of their sides, as the shader leads them), the lead running along the network twice as fast as anything spreads straight out from the click, so it races round the leading; each separate piece of leading starts where it comes nearest the click. Then the last light passes outward from the click through the glass, each pane flaring as it takes it, and the window settles into its night.

algorithms.name: Colour negative film
algorithms.what: The page is exposed onto 35 mm film: inverted, under the orange mask colour negatives carry, with sprocket holes along its edges and lines between its frames. Its frames then come up as positive prints in the developer.

algorithms.name: A twisting helix (a framed curve)
algorithms.what: Each strip of film is pulled off the table along a rising helix: its frame (tangent, width, face) is carried along the curve and turned about the tangent, so the ribbon twists as it coils up the screen.

algorithms.name: A blur the vortex sharpens
algorithms.what: The cubes bring Science in heavily blurred, read from a mipmap pyramid of the page (a coarser level the blurrier, in five samples). The vortex’s wide base ring sharpens it: the foot of the screen first, while the vortex stands there, then, once the gathering is done, the whole page from the bottom up as the base lifts and its ring climbs, the blur shrinking continuously under the arch of its tendrils.

algorithms.name: The Lorenz attractor
algorithms.what: Each thrown cube swerves along its own stretch of Lorenz’s chaotic system (σ = 10, ρ = 28, β = 8/3), integrated as it flies and pinned to nothing at its release and its landing, so no two throws curve alike.

algorithms.name: Damped ripples
algorithms.what: Developer ripples spread out from the line where the film lifts, dying away with distance, under the safelight.

algorithms.name: Diffraction spikes
algorithms.what: A nine-bladed aperture spreads a point of light into eighteen spikes, two for each blade edge.

algorithms.name: Kepler’s third law and transit photometry
algorithms.what: TRAPPIST-1’s seven planets at their measured periods; each one crossing the star dims it by the share of its disc it covers, (Rp / R★)².

algorithms.name: Topological flocking
algorithms.what: Each starling aligns with, steers toward and keeps clear of its seven nearest neighbours, however far they are (Ballerini et al. 2008); the murmuration’s shape comes out of that.

algorithms.name: Extrapolating Voyager 1
algorithms.what: Its distance from one reference point and its speed (about 17 km/s), and the light-travel time that distance implies.

algorithms.name: Value noise and fractal Brownian motion
algorithms.what: Hashed lattice noise summed over octaves: the paper’s grain, the nebula, the supernova remnants’ filaments (in three dimensions, the valleys of turbulence), the ink ridges, the developer tray, the fog on history steps.

algorithms.name: Domain warping
algorithms.what: Noise fed into noise, which folds the nebula into filaments.

algorithms.name: Voronoi cells
algorithms.what: Each point belongs to its nearest seeded nucleus. Voronoi cells shape the caustics under Racing’s glacier, the cells (in Jeans lengths) a remnant’s gas falls into its clumps from, and the crowns of the White Mountains’ forest, each a tree.

algorithms.name: Recursive branching
algorithms.what: A few trunks that fork three times, each level twice as many branches as the last, wobbled by noise; the ink fills in nearest its branches first.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Chess, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Streamline integration
algorithms.what: Ink strokes traced step by step along the vortex field (Euler integration), tapering as they go.

algorithms.name: Halftone screening
algorithms.what: Tone as dots on a 45° screen, each as large as the tone it stands for; the screen grows finer as the print develops.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Photography: the prints developing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Ordered dithering
algorithms.what: An 8 × 8 Bayer threshold matrix built by interleaving bits; levels rise from 2 to 32 per channel before the print reaches full tone.

algorithms.name: Time scales and arc length
algorithms.what: The Power Map places 224 moments by date along one line; the Birkie route is drawn to the point the race clock has reached, by arc length along its path.
algorithms.where: The homepage’s About Me band, Racing

algorithms.name: Vogel’s phyllotaxis
algorithms.what: Seed n sits at radius c√n, turned n times the golden angle (137.508°); the seeds pack without gaps in 34 and 55 spirals.

algorithms.name: Barnsley’s fern
algorithms.what: An iterated function system: four affine maps, picked at random, draw a fern made of smaller ferns.

algorithms.name: The Drake equation
algorithms.what: The number of civilisations we could hear from as a product of seven factors, set on log scales where they span orders of magnitude.

algorithms.name: Signed distance fields
algorithms.what: Shapes as distance functions, so their edges stay sharp at any size: the glass card, the iris blades, the maze’s corridors, the crystal on the homepage.

algorithms.name: Metaballs
algorithms.what: The liquid-chrome drops are one implicit surface, the sum of r² / d² from each centre; its gradient gives the normal, so drops merge as they touch.

algorithms.name: Perspective projection and back-face culling
algorithms.what: Cubes fly toward a camera in front of the screen, faces turned away skipped instead of sorted; the White Mountains are seen through a pinhole camera that flies.

algorithms.name: Marching squares on a module
algorithms.what: Outdoors’ window leads the White Mountains’ heights, stepped into bands, on a square module 1.6 km on a side: each band’s edge is marching squares on the module’s corners with its vertices at the edges’ midpoints, so every line of came runs square or at 45°, Wright’s Prairie geometry; a saddle is settled by the module’s middle. Where three or more edges meet the joint is soldered.

algorithms.name: Light through art glass
algorithms.what: Outdoors’ world is the White Mountains as a Frank Lloyd Wright window seen from inside as night falls. What comes through each pane is the light outside times the glass’s transmission: the lowland clear antique glass, as his fields are, a little wavy (it refracts what is behind it) and seedy with bubbles; the colour gathered on the mountains, sage and forest green, cream opalescent that scatters the light and takes up the lantern’s, iridized gold; each summit a Cherokee-red square (neighbours share a rectangle), each named tarn an iridized jewel. Outside, the last light low behind far trees and the shadows of leaves drifting across the glass; once it has gone the colour glows only faintly, the red like embers, and the lantern brings it up where it passes; the light halates over the came, and the lantern (your pointer) catches its crown and the solder. Drawn from a 32 KB plate of the heights, the moment a page opens.

algorithms.name: An iris aperture
algorithms.what: Nine curved blades as a signed distance field around the click, turning as they close; out-of-focus highlights take the aperture’s nine-sided shape (bokeh).

algorithms.name: A faceted gem
algorithms.what: The homepage crystal: six facets, each a window refracted toward its own corner of a destination’s world, with prism edges and a spectrum cast on the paper.
